meta.title: Smooth Muscle
meta.summary: Smooth muscle is the quiet muscle — it lines your gut, bladder, airways, blood vessels and uterus, and works every hour of your life without you ever noticing.

sections.title: Smooth Muscle — Built for Endurance, Not Speed
Smooth Muscle Contraction — A Completely Different Trigger
All Three Muscle Types, Side by Side
Smooth Muscle — Built for Endurance, Not Speed

items: Smooth muscle is the quiet muscle — it lines your gut, bladder, airways, blood vessels and uterus, and works every hour of your life without you ever noticing.
It is built for the opposite job to skeletal muscle: not speed and power, but slow, sustained, extremely cheap tension.
Its trigger is genuinely different: there is no troponin. Calcium works through calmodulin instead, and the switch is on the myosin side rather than the actin side.
Its trademark trick is the latch state — holding tension for hours while burning almost no ATP.
Cells are small, spindle-shaped, with a single central nucleus — nothing like the long multinucleated skeletal fibre.
No striations, because the filaments run diagonally in criss-crossing bundles rather than in neat sarcomeres. It still has actin and myosin — just untidily arranged.
Dense bodies do the job Z lines do elsewhere: they anchor thin filaments and are tied together by intermediate filaments, so the whole cell twists and shortens like a wrung cloth.
Far more thin filaments per thick filament than skeletal muscle — one reason it can shorten so dramatically.
Caveolae are surface pockets that act like a simple substitute for T-tubules.
It answers to almost everything: autonomic nerves, hormones, local chemicals, and plain stretch — not to voluntary command.
Smooth muscle in your gut is working right now, moving your last meal along, and you cannot feel it or stop it.
Goosebumps are tiny smooth muscles pulling on hair follicles — a rare case where you can actually see smooth muscle working.

blocks.x: If skeletal muscle is a sprinter and cardiac muscle is a metronome, smooth muscle is the patient, tireless worker lining your gut, blood vessels, and airways — squeezing slowly and steadily for hours without you ever noticing. It looks nothing like the other two muscle types under a microscope, and that's because its job is completely different.

blocks.cap: A smooth muscle cell: spindle-shaped, one nucleus, dense bodies, caveolae.

blocks.name: Smooth muscle cells — general arrangement
blocks.def: Found in SHEETS lining the walls of hollow organs. Individual cells are spindle-shaped, with one centrally-placed nucleus per cell, and lots of mitochondria.

blocks.name: Smooth muscle striation
blocks.def: NOT striated — this is its defining visual difference from skeletal and cardiac muscle. Most of the sarcoplasm is filled with contractile filaments, interrupted by structures called focal densities.

blocks.name: Thin filaments in smooth muscle
blocks.def: Composed of <term d="The thin filament protein that the thick filaments grab and pull on during contraction.">actin</term> with tropomyosin — but critically, NO troponin is present in smooth muscle cells at all. This is a fundamental difference from skeletal and cardiac muscle, and it's exactly why smooth muscle needs a completely different calcium-sensing mechanism (see Contraction section below).

blocks.name: Dense bodies
blocks.def: Found in the cytoplasm or at the cell membrane, dense bodies are the organizational sites where thick and thin filaments interact and are anchored. They contain the protein alpha-actinin and are functionally SIMILAR to the Z lines of striated muscle — smooth muscle's version of an anchor point, just without the organized <term d="The basic contracting unit of a muscle fibre, running from one Z-line to the next.">sarcomere</term> structure.

blocks.name: Thin-to-thick filament ratio
blocks.def: Much HIGHER in smooth muscle (about 15:1) than in skeletal muscle (about 6:1) — smooth muscle packs in proportionally far more actin relative to <term d="The thick filament protein whose heads pull on actin to shorten the muscle.">myosin</term>.

blocks.name: Intermediate filaments in smooth muscle
blocks.def: Non-contractile filaments containing the proteins desmin or vimentin — they help relay the contraction force through the cell and help the cell shorten as a whole.

blocks.name: Caveolae
blocks.def: Numerous invaginations of the <term d="The straw-coloured liquid part of blood that carries the cells, proteins, nutrients and wastes.">plasma</term> membrane at the periphery of smooth muscle cells, believed to help bring in calcium needed for contraction. Functionally EQUIVALENT to the T-tubule system of striated muscle, though structurally quite different (small pouches rather than deep tubules).

blocks.name: Smooth muscle fiber size
blocks.def: Much smaller (2-10 micrometers in diameter) than skeletal muscle fibers (10-100 micrometers) — smooth muscle cells are noticeably tinier.

blocks.name: <term d="The muscle cell's internal calcium store, released to trigger contraction.">Sarcoplasmic reticulum</term> in smooth muscle
blocks.def: Very little SR compared to skeletal or even cardiac muscle — another reason smooth muscle depends heavily on extracellular calcium entry (via caveolae and channels) rather than internal SR stores.

blocks.name: Cell-to-cell connections in smooth muscle
blocks.def: Smooth muscle cells are linked by desmosomes (mechanical junctions, providing structural strength) and gap junctions (electrical junctions, allowing coordinated activity between cells).

blocks.name: What controls smooth muscle
blocks.def: The autonomic nervous system, hormones, metabolites, and drugs — a notably WIDER range of controlling inputs than skeletal muscle (which responds only to its motor neuron) or even cardiac muscle.

blocks.x: ▶️What Controls Smooth MusclesVideo · Non Stop Neurone

items: Multiunit: cells act individually, each with its own nerve supply — built for precision. Found in the iris, ciliary muscle of the eye, and large airways.
Visceral (unitary): cells are joined by gap junctions and contract as a sheet — built for bulk movement. Found in gut, bladder, uterus and small vessels.
Visceral smooth muscle shows slow wave potentials — rhythmic drifts in membrane potential that fire off contractions when they reach threshold. It is self-pacing, like the heart.
It also responds to stretch by contracting, meaning a full organ automatically tends to empty itself.
Multiunit = your pupil narrowing in bright sunlight — fine, graded, precise.
Visceral = the wave of a swallow travelling down, or the cramping waves of gut upset — coordinated sheets, not single cells.

blocks.x: Not all smooth muscle behaves the same way. Some behaves like a bundle of independent soldiers, each needing its own individual order; other smooth muscle behaves like a single unit that moves together the instant one part gets the signal.

blocks.name: Multiunit smooth muscle
blocks.def: Made up of discrete, SEPARATE smooth muscle fibers, consisting of motor units activated by nervous stimulation (much like skeletal muscle, in this one respect). Found in the walls of large blood vessels, in the eye (ciliary body), and at the base of hair follicles (the muscles that produce 'goose bumps'). Has high innervation density, no interconnecting bridges between cells, a stable <term d="The difference in electrical charge between the inside and outside of a cell membrane.">membrane potential</term> with no spontaneous <term d="A shift of the membrane potential toward zero — the inside of the cell becomes less negative.">depolarization</term>, and typically does NOT display action potentials when stimulated to contract.

blocks.name: Visceral (unitary) smooth muscle
blocks.def: Made up of fibers bound together to function as a SINGLE unit. Found in the walls of hollow organs — small blood vessels, the digestive tract, urinary system, and reproductive system. Multiple fibers contract AS ONE UNIT because impulses travel easily cell-to-cell across gap junctions.

blocks.name: Slow wave potentials (pacemaker activity)
blocks.def: In some cases, visceral smooth muscle is self-excitable — generating spontaneous, graded, rhythmical oscillations in membrane potential called slow wave potentials, or pacemaker activity. This is conceptually similar to the SA node's automaticity in cardiac muscle, but occurring in smooth muscle organs like the gut.

blocks.name: Other properties of visceral smooth muscle
blocks.def: Low innervation density (unlike multiunit's high density); exhibits PLASTICITY (can maintain tension even as it's stretched, adapting its length); and contracts when stretched — a property called myogenic activity, meaning the stretch itself, not a nerve signal, is what triggers the contraction.

sections.title: Smooth Muscle Contraction — A Completely Different Trigger

items: The trigger is still calcium, but the target is different: there is no troponin in smooth muscle.
Calcium binds calmodulin → the calcium–calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) → MLCK phosphorylates the myosin head → only then can myosin bind actin.
So remember the flip: skeletal/cardiac regulation is on the thin (actin) filament; smooth muscle regulation is on the thick (myosin) filament.
Calcium can arrive from outside the cell, from internal stores (via IP₃), or through receptor-driven pathways — which is why so many different signals can make smooth muscle contract.
Switching off requires myosin light chain phosphatase to remove the phosphate. Contraction and relaxation are therefore a tug-of-war between a kinase and a phosphatase.
The latch mechanism: crossbridges cycle so slowly that they stay attached, holding tension for long periods at almost no ATP cost.
Latch is why your blood vessels hold tone all day without exhausting themselves — skeletal muscle attempting that would fatigue in minutes.
Asthma inhalers (salbutamol) work exactly here — they relax airway smooth muscle by shifting that kinase/phosphatase balance.
Most blood-pressure drugs are, at bottom, drugs that persuade vascular smooth muscle to relax.

blocks.x: Since smooth muscle has no troponin, it can't use the calcium-troponin trigger that skeletal and cardiac muscle rely on. Instead, it uses an entirely different calcium-sensing protein — calmodulin — and an enzyme that chemically tags the myosin itself before it's allowed to work.

blocks.cap: The six-step calcium-calmodulin pathway that triggers smooth muscle contraction.

blocks.name: Trigger for smooth muscle contraction
blocks.def: Contractions are initiated by agents that INCREASE intracellular [Ca2+]. Smooth muscle has relatively FEW voltage-gated Na+ channels compared to other excitable cells — instead, the flow of Ca2+ into the cell is mainly responsible for generating any <term d="A brief, all-or-nothing electrical signal that sweeps along a nerve or muscle cell.">action potential</term> that does occur.

blocks.name: Three ways intracellular calcium can be increased
blocks.def: Opening of voltage-gated calcium (L-type) channels as a result of <term d="The cell membrane of a muscle fibre.">sarcolemma</term> depolarization; calcium-induced calcium influx; and receptor-mediated calcium mobilization.

blocks.name: Receptor-mediated calcium mobilization — two pathways
blocks.def: Ligand-gated Ca2+ channels (<term d="A protein that recognises and binds a specific signal molecule, triggering a response in the cell.">receptor</term> occupancy directly opens Ca2+ channels in the sarcolemma, causing Ca2+ influx from the ECF) and intracellular mobilization via IP3 (resulting in Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through inositol trisphosphate receptor channels) — the same IP3 second-messenger system covered in <term d="The body's ability to keep its internal conditions steady despite changes going on outside.">Homeostasis</term>, reused here for a muscular purpose.

blocks.name: Calmodulin (CaM) — smooth muscle's calcium sensor
blocks.def: Since there's no troponin in smooth muscle, free Ca2+ instead binds to calmodulin, in a ratio of 4 calcium ions to 1 calmodulin molecule — smooth muscle's substitute calcium-sensing protein.

blocks.name: Caldesmon
blocks.def: A protein that, in the RESTING state, binds to the tropomyosin/actin complex and BLOCKS myosin from binding actin, keeping the muscle relaxed. When calcium-calmodulin (CaCM) binds caldesmon, it is released from the tropomyosin/actin complex, finally allowing myosin to bind the thin filament — functionally similar to what troponin/tropomyosin does in skeletal muscle, just using different proteins.

blocks.name: Myosin Light Chain Kinase (MLCK)
blocks.def: Activated by the calcium-calmodulin (CaCM) complex. MLCK phosphorylates the myosin light chains (MLC), using ATP. This phosphorylation event is what INCREASES myosin ATPase activity — in smooth muscle, myosin itself must be chemically switched on before contraction can proceed, unlike skeletal/cardiac muscle where myosin is always 'ready' and it's actin's exposure that's regulated instead.

blocks.name: Crossbridge cycling in smooth muscle
blocks.def: Once activated (phosphorylated), crossbridges cycle in the SAME basic fashion as in striated muscle — but the cycling is considerably SLOWER in smooth muscle than in skeletal muscle, consistent with smooth muscle's role in slow, sustained, energy-efficient contraction rather than fast, powerful movement.

blocks.name: Myosin-light-chain phosphatase
blocks.def: The enzyme responsible for DEphosphorylating myosin light chains once intracellular Ca2+ decreases — reversing what MLCK did, and turning the contraction machinery back off.

blocks.name: The latchbridge mechanism
blocks.def: Dephosphorylated myosin light chains have a very LOW affinity for the ATP needed to break the actin-myosin crosslinkage — so the myosin heads that remain attached can hold force at the muscle's ends for a prolonged period with minimal ATP expenditure. This is called the smooth muscle latchbridge mechanism, and it's precisely why smooth muscle (e.g., in blood vessels or sphincters) can maintain steady tone for hours without exhausting its energy supply, unlike skeletal muscle.

items: Relaxation needs calcium removal and the phosphatase to strip the phosphate off myosin.
Its length–tension behaviour is unusual: smooth muscle can generate force across a very wide range of lengths, instead of only near one optimum.
Stress relaxation (plasticity): stretch it and tension rises — then gradually fades back down even though it is still stretched.
That property is what lets hollow organs fill up without the pressure inside climbing.
Your bladder fills steadily for hours, yet the urge does not rise steadily — pressure keeps settling back. That is stress relaxation, and without it you would need the toilet constantly.
The same property lets the stomach accept a large meal, and the uterus expand across a pregnancy.

blocks.name: Smooth muscle relaxation
blocks.def: Associated with LOW intracellular Ca2+ concentrations. Low Ca2+ is achieved through Ca2+ extrusion from the cell using the 3Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and the sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase, PLUS reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via the sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase — several parallel routes work together to clear calcium and allow relaxation.

blocks.name: Smooth muscle's unusual length-tension behavior
blocks.def: When stretched, smooth muscle shows a transient large force (resistance to stretch) that then DECAYS to a new, constant, lower level within minutes — a phenomenon called stress relaxation. As a result, it is essentially impossible to correlate length and tension accurately in smooth muscle the way you can in skeletal or cardiac muscle, and smooth muscle has no true fixed 'resting length' the way striated muscle does.

blocks.name: Stress relaxation — why it matters functionally
blocks.def: This property allows organs like the bladder or stomach to accommodate a large increase in volume (being stretched considerably) without a proportional, ever-increasing rise in internal pressure — the smooth muscle wall 'gives' and settles to a new baseline tension rather than fighting the stretch indefinitely.

sections.title: All Three Muscle Types, Side by Side

blocks.title: The comparison that ties the trio together

items: Striations: skeletal ✔, cardiac ✔, smooth ✘.
Nuclei: skeletal many; cardiac usually one; smooth one.
Control: skeletal voluntary; cardiac and smooth involuntary.
Troponin: present in skeletal and cardiac; absent in smooth (calmodulin instead).
Speed: skeletal fast, cardiac intermediate, smooth slow — but smooth is by far the most economical.
Tetanus: possible in skeletal; impossible in cardiac; smooth sustains tension by latch instead.
Electrical coupling: absent in skeletal; present in cardiac; present in visceral (not multiunit) smooth muscle.
Automaticity: none in skeletal; strong in cardiac; present in visceral smooth muscle (slow waves).

blocks.title: One sentence to hold all three

items: Skeletal = sprinter (fast, powerful, tires, waits for orders). Cardiac = metronome (tireless, self-starting, never cramps). Smooth = marathon walker (slow, cheap, holds on forever).

blocks.x: You've now covered all three muscle types across three separate topics. Here they are pulled together into direct three-way comparisons — this is exactly the kind of table that tends to show up as exam questions.
▶️Smooth Muscles vs Skeletal MusclesVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Striation: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — striated (clear bands). Cardiac — striated, but less distinct bands. Smooth — NOT striated at all, no visible banding.

blocks.name: Nuclei: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — multiple nuclei, peripherally located. Cardiac — one nucleus (mononucleate), centrally located. Smooth — one nucleus (mononucleate), centrally located.

blocks.name: Control: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — voluntary. Cardiac — involuntary. Smooth — involuntary.

blocks.name: Presence of troponin: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — present, the primary calcium sensor. Cardiac — present, same role as skeletal muscle. Smooth — ABSENT entirely; calmodulin takes over the calcium-sensing role instead.

blocks.name: Speed of contraction: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — fast. Cardiac — moderate, rhythmic. Smooth — slow and sustained, but highly energy-efficient (via the latchbridge mechanism).

blocks.name: Ability to be tetanized: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — CAN be tetanized (<term d="A short spell straight after firing when the cell cannot fire again, or needs a stronger stimulus.">refractory period</term> is short relative to twitch duration). Cardiac — CANNOT be tetanized (refractory period outlasts the twitch, a functional necessity for pumping). Smooth — sustains prolonged contraction naturally via the latchbridge mechanism, without needing rapid restimulation the way skeletal <term d="A smooth, sustained contraction produced when stimuli arrive too fast for the muscle to relax in between.">tetanus</term> does.

blocks.name: Cell-to-cell electrical connection: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — none; each fiber is independently activated by its own <term d="The synapse where a motor nerve meets a muscle fibre.">neuromuscular junction</term>. Cardiac — gap junctions at intercalated discs connect all cells into an electrical <term d="A group of cells joined so closely that they respond electrically as a single unit.">syncytium</term>. Smooth — gap junctions connect cells in visceral (unitary) smooth muscle, allowing it to act as a unit; multiunit smooth muscle lacks this connection, behaving more like skeletal muscle in this one respect.

blocks.name: Main calcium source for contraction: skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — almost entirely from the well-developed sarcoplasmic reticulum. Cardiac — both extracellular entry AND SR release (calcium-induced calcium release), since the SR is less developed. Smooth — extracellular entry (via caveolae and channels) plus IP3-triggered release from a sparse SR.

blocks.name: Automaticity (self-generated rhythm): skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth
blocks.def: Skeletal — none; always requires a nerve signal to contract. Cardiac — YES, in pacemaker tissue (SA node etc.), which generates its own spontaneous rhythm. Smooth — YES, in visceral (unitary) smooth muscle, via slow wave potentials/pacemaker activity; multiunit smooth muscle lacks this and requires nervous stimulation like skeletal muscle.

items: No troponin → calmodulin instead. The single most testable fact in this topic.
Regulation is on the thick filament (myosin) in smooth muscle, but on the thin filament (actin) in skeletal and cardiac.
Ca²⁺ → calmodulin → MLCK → phosphorylated myosin → contraction. Learn that chain in order.
Latch = tension held cheaply, for hours, on very little ATP.
Multiunit = precision (eye); visceral = sheets (gut, bladder).

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: Smooth muscle does have actin and myosin. It lacks striations because the filaments are not arranged in neat sarcomeres — not because the proteins are missing.
Slow does not mean weak. Smooth muscle generates considerable force and sustains it far longer than skeletal muscle could.
Stress relaxation is not fatigue. The muscle is not tiring — tension deliberately settles so hollow organs can fill without pressure rising.
Contraction and relaxation are a kinase/phosphatase tug-of-war, not a simple on/off switch.
← Skeletal & Cardiac Muscle (Topics 04–05): the same actin and myosin appear a third time — only the switch and the arrangement have changed.
← Homeostasis (Topic 02): the calcium–calmodulin–MLCK route is textbook signal transduction, complete with second messengers and amplification.
→ Autonomic Nervous System (Topic 09): smooth muscle is the ANS's main effector. Every receptor you meet there acts on the pathway you just learned here.
→ Blood & CVS (Topic 08): vascular smooth muscle tone is what sets blood pressure and directs blood where it is needed.
The one-line summary: no troponin, no striations, no hurry — calcium works through calmodulin, and the latch state holds tension almost for free.

lines: Calcium binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase; relaxation waits on the phosphatase, not on calcium alone.

mnemonics.h: Single unit gut, multi unit eye
lines: Visceral smooth muscle is electrically coupled and spontaneously active; multi-unit fibres are separately innervated for fine, graded control.
Smooth muscle holds tone for long stretches on very little ATP, which is why blood vessels and sphincters can stay contracted for hours.

mnemonics.h: Slow to start, slow to stop
lines: Contraction and relaxation take far longer than in skeletal muscle, but the tension produced per unit of energy is far higher.
